conditions.name: Common cold (upper respiratory tract infection)

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: A self-limiting viral infection of the nose and throat. Blocked and runny nose, sneezing, mild sore throat, and a cough that appears a few days in.
workup: Review if symptoms last beyond 10 days or fever returns

exam.positive: Diffuse erythema without exudate
Their presence points away from streptococcus

conditions.name: Viral pharyngitis

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: The commonest cause of a sore throat by far. Comes with a cough, runny nose and hoarseness, which is precisely what distinguishes it from strep.

exam.positive: Normal, or scattered wheeze clearing with cough
Focal crackles or dullness point to pneumonia instead
Normal observations support a self-limiting course

triage.label: Self-care

Clear chest distinguishes it from pneumonia

triage.label: See a doctor soon

Chest X-ray if secondary pneumonia suspected

conditions.name: Acute sinusitis

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: Inflamed sinuses following a cold. Facial pressure worse on bending forward, a blocked nose and a reduced sense of smell, typically after day ten of a cold.
workup: Antibiotics only if severe or worsening after 10 days

exam.positive: A fall of 3% or more on exertion is significant

exam.positive: Above 20 warrants review

triage.label: See a doctor soon

Dullness over the affected zone

exam.positive: Documented weight loss

exam.positive: Grunting, nasal flaring, severe recession or apnoea need urgent hospital assessment
Poor feeding is a key marker of severity in an infant, alongside oxygen saturation
Wheeze and/or fine crackles, without the barking cough/stridor of croup

conditions.name: Bronchiolitis

triage.label: Urgent
triage.action: Seek medical assessment today

conditions.summary: An infant (usually under 2, peak 3-6 months) with coryzal symptoms progressing to cough, wheeze and increased work of breathing, often with poor feeding -- usually viral (RSV). A very common infant presentation to Indian paediatric OPDs/EDs, especially in cooler months, and distinct enough from adult bronchitis/asthma to need its own entry. Apnoea, marked respiratory distress (grunting, nasal flaring, severe recession), or a low oxygen saturation need urgent hospital assessment.
workup: Supportive care: fluids, minimal handling, oxygen if needed
No proven benefit from bronchodilators, steroids or antibiotics in typical bronchiolitis
Pulse oximetry to guide the admission decision
Admit if red flags or feeding poorly

exam.positive: Recurrent, variable episodes of wheeze/cough/breathlessness rather than a single ongoing flare

exam.positive: Nocturnal cough/wheeze and exercise-induced symptoms are characteristic
Increasing reliever use signals poor control and exacerbation risk

Variability over time supports the diagnosis and tracks control

conditions.name: Chronic stable asthma

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Recurrent wheeze, cough (often nocturnal or exercise-induced), chest tightness and breathlessness, variable over time and often with an atopic history -- the ongoing, day-to-day condition, distinct from this app's existing acute-flare entry. Air-pollution burden in Indian cities is a major, often under-addressed trigger and driver of poor control. Increasing reliever-inhaler use, night-time symptoms, or a falling peak flow signal poor control and risk of exacerbation.
workup: Spirometry with reversibility testing, peak flow diary, FeNO if available
Inhaled corticosteroid +/- long-acting beta-agonist, stepped per GINA/BTS guidance
Address triggers, including air pollution exposure

exam.step: Ask about smoking AND biomass/occupational smoke exposure explicitly
exam.positive: Either history supports the diagnosis -- biomass exposure is a major cause in non-smoking Indian women
Slowly progressive breathlessness and cough over months to years, not a single acute flare
Worsening despite treatment needs reassessment for exacerbation or an alternative diagnosis (e.g. bronchiectasis, lung cancer)

labs.confirms: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 confirms fixed airflow obstruction
If young or non-smoker, screens for a genetic cause

conditions.name: Chronic stable COPD

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Progressive breathlessness with a chronic productive cough, in a smoker or someone with heavy biomass/occupational smoke exposure, usually over 40 -- the ongoing, day-to-day condition, distinct from this app's existing acute-flare entry. Biomass cooking-fuel smoke (wood, dung, crop residue) is a major driver in Indian women who have never smoked, a genuinely different at-risk group than the 'smoker' stereotype. Worsening despite treatment needs re-assessment for an exacerbation or an alternative diagnosis.
workup: Spirometry (post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 confirms the diagnosis)
Alpha-1 antitrypsin level if young or a non-smoker
Smoking/biomass-smoke cessation is the single most effective intervention

exam.step: Ask about sputum volume and character
exam.positive: Large volumes of often purulent sputum daily is the defining feature
Post-TB bronchiectasis is a distinctly common cause in India -- ask explicitly rather than assuming a congenital cause
Significant haemoptysis needs urgent assessment

labs.confirms: Underlying-cause work-up where no post-infective/post-TB cause is evident

conditions.name: Bronchiectasis

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Chronic productive cough with large volumes of often purulent sputum, recurrent chest infections, and sometimes haemoptysis -- often post-infective, and post-tuberculosis bronchiectasis is a distinctly common cause in India given the country's TB burden, unlike the Western congenital/cystic-fibrosis-driven cause profile most checkers assume. Significant haemoptysis needs urgent assessment; recurrent fevers with worsening sputum suggest an infective exacerbation needing antibiotics.
workup: Consider underlying-cause work-up (immunoglobulins, cystic fibrosis, ciliary dysfunction) -- and specifically ask about past TB in Indian patients
Treat exacerbations promptly with antibiotics guided by sputum culture
Address the underlying cause where identifiable

exam.step: Ask specifically about a characteristic inspiratory 'whoop' after coughing fits, or vomiting after coughing
exam.positive: Post-tussive vomiting and the whoop are real hallmarks -- no dedicated evidence node captures either directly, so this is assessed by history

exam.step: Ask how long the cough has lasted
exam.positive: A cough persisting for weeks, well beyond a typical viral illness, is characteristic -- the '100-day cough'
Fever is usually low-grade or absent in pertussis -- its prominent presence should raise suspicion of Croup, Bronchiolitis or pneumonia instead

labs.confirms: The standard confirmatory test, most sensitive in the first 2-3 weeks of illness
Reasonable in a known outbreak with the classic paroxysmal, prolonged cough pattern

conditions.name: Whooping cough

triage.label: Urgent
triage.action: Seek medical assessment today

conditions.summary: A prolonged, paroxysmal cough illness -- severe coughing fits, sometimes ending in a characteristic inspiratory 'whoop' or post-tussive vomiting (no dedicated evidence node captures the whoop or vomiting directly, carried in the exam narrative), lasting weeks to months (the '100-day cough'). Notably, fever is usually low-grade or absent -- a real distinguishing feature from Croup or Bronchiolitis, which typically have a more prominent fever. Occurs in unvaccinated/under-vaccinated children AND in adults with waning vaccine immunity, who can then transmit it to vulnerable unvaccinated infants -- the group at real risk of apnoea and severe complications.
workup: Nasopharyngeal swab PCR for Bordetella pertussis
Notify public health -- pertussis is a notifiable disease in most jurisdictions
A macrolide antibiotic (azithromycin 3-5 days, or clarithromycin/erythromycin) -- reduces transmission but does NOT shorten the illness once established, an honestly-nuanced point
Urgent assessment for any young infant with suspected pertussis, given real apnoea/complication risk
Ensure close contacts, especially pregnant women and young infants, are appropriately protected/vaccinated

exam.step: Ask about tobacco use pattern (smoked and/or smokeless), duration, and readiness to quit
exam.positive: The single most important assessment -- no dedicated evidence node captures a structured dependence-severity score directly, so this is assessed by history

exam.step: Ask specifically about breathlessness, unintentional weight loss, coughing blood, or night sweats, looking for their ABSENCE
exam.positive: Their presence should prompt considering COPD, lung cancer or TB instead of simple dependence -- these should genuinely be absent here

exam.step: Assess motivation and previous quit attempts
exam.positive: Informs the appropriate intensity of counselling and pharmacotherapy support offered

labs.confirms: Usually sufficient for diagnosis -- the key investigations are for excluding smoking-related complications, not confirming dependence itself

labs.test: Chest X-ray/spirometry if red flags are present
labs.confirms: Reserved for excluding COPD, lung cancer or TB when red-flag symptoms are present

conditions.name: Tobacco / nicotine dependence

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Dependence on tobacco (smoked or smokeless, both genuinely common in India) -- often presenting as a chronic 'smoker's cough' without yet having developed established lung damage. Distinct from COPD, Lung Cancer or TB sharing this bundle, all of which are also linked to smoking: this condition specifically models straightforward dependence, where red-flag findings (significant breathlessness, weight loss, coughing blood, night sweats) should be genuinely absent -- their presence should prompt looking for one of those more serious conditions instead, not just attributing everything to 'being a smoker'.
workup: Ask specifically about quantity, frequency and duration of tobacco use (smoked and/or smokeless), and past quit attempts
Behavioural counselling combined with pharmacotherapy (nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline, or bupropion) -- genuinely more effective together than either alone
Screen for and address red flags (weight loss, haemoptysis, significant breathlessness, night sweats) that would suggest COPD, lung cancer or TB instead of simple dependence
Offer a clear quit date and follow-up support -- structured cessation support genuinely improves success rates over unsupported attempts

redFlags.label: Possible sepsis
redFlags.message: A fever together with confusion, very fast breathing, mottled skin or a collapsing blood pressure can mean infection is affecting the whole body.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

redFlags.label: Rash that does not fade under pressure
redFlags.message: Spots that stay visible when a glass is pressed on them, alongside feeling unwell, can be a sign of bacteria in the bloodstream.

redFlags.label: Possible severe allergic reaction
redFlags.message: Swelling of the throat or tongue with difficulty breathing after a food, sting, or medicine can close the airway within minutes.
redFlags.action: Use an adrenaline auto-injector if you have one, then call emergency services.

redFlags.label: Reduced consciousness
redFlags.message: Being difficult to rouse, or drifting in and out of awareness, always needs immediate assessment whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Place the person on their side if unresponsive.

redFlags.label: Severe breathing difficulty
redFlags.message: An oxygen level below 94 percent, or being unable to speak a full sentence, means the lungs are not keeping up.

redFlags.label: Possible stroke
redFlags.message: Sudden facial drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking is a stroke until proven otherwise. Treatment works only within a few hours.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now and note the exact time symptoms began.

redFlags.label: Seizure
redFlags.message: A first seizure needs assessment to find the cause and to advise on driving and safety.
redFlags.action: Seek urgent assessment today. Call emergency services if the seizure lasted over five minutes or a second one followed.

redFlags.label: Significant gastrointestinal bleeding
redFlags.message: Vomiting blood, or passing black tarry stools, means bleeding inside the digestive tract.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now.

redFlags.label: New jaundice
redFlags.message: Yellowing of the skin or eyes always needs blood tests to find out why.

redFlags.label: Sudden loss of vision
redFlags.message: Sight lost suddenly in one or both eyes needs assessment the same hour, whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Go to an eye emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Coughing up blood
redFlags.message: Coughing up blood always needs a chest X-ray, particularly in a smoker or former smoker.
redFlags.action: Seek medical assessment within 24 hours for a chest X-ray.

redFlags.label: Persistent cough with weight loss
redFlags.message: A cough lasting over three weeks with weight loss or night sweats needs imaging to exclude serious lung disease.
redFlags.action: Arrange a chest X-ray and medical review within two weeks.

redFlags.label: Thoughts of self-harm
redFlags.message: Thoughts of harming yourself or of being better off dead deserve help today. You do not have to be in crisis to reach out.
redFlags.action: Contact your doctor, a crisis line, or go to an emergency department now. If you are in immediate danger, call emergency services.

redFlags.label: New confusion coming on over hours or days
redFlags.message: Confusion that has come on over hours or days, or that comes and goes through the day, is delirium until proven otherwise. It is caused by something else -- an infection, a drug, pain, retention -- and that cause needs finding today.
redFlags.action: Seek same-day medical assessment. Take a list of all medications. Call emergency services if they are drowsy, feverish or cannot be roused properly.

disclaimer: This tool provides information about possible causes of symptoms. It is not a diagnosis and it cannot examine you. It does not replace assessment by a qualified clinician. If you feel very unwell, or your symptoms are getting rapidly worse, seek medical help immediately regardless of what this tool says.
